classification_signals: Preface states 'This book looks at city forests primarily from a cultural and social perspective.' and 'It is based on many journeys, excursions, talks with city forest managers and users, as well as formal studies by many colleagues, myself, and a series of talented undergraduate and graduate students.' (p. 7). The table of contents lists chapters covering historical, social, cultural, and environmental aspects of urban forests, indicating a broad synthesis and conceptual development rather than a single empirical study (p. 10).
title: The Forest and the City: The Cultural Landscape of Urban Woodland

findings.consequent: Space (unknown, wild, adventurous)
findings.quote: Where place refers to home, familiarity and safety, space represents for the unknown, the wild, the adventurous (Tuan 2007).

findings.antecedent: Idea of landscape, myth, vision established in actual place
findings.consequent: Muddled categories, metaphors become real, part of scenery
findings.quote: once a cer tain idea of landscape, a myth, a vision, establishes itself in an actual place, it has a peculiar way of muddling categories, of making metaphors more real than their referents; of becoming, in fact, part of the scenery.

findings.consequent: Environmental influence on behavior, behavioral influence on environment
findings.quote: Many experts see urbanisation as the most impor tant environmental influence on behaviour, as well as the most important behav ioural influence on the environment (Gallagher 1993).

findings.consequent: Role in aristocratic/bourgeois leisure, symbols of nature, links to human-natural world relationship
findings.quote: Trees played a crucial role in aristocratic leisure, and later in a bourgeois sense of gentility... Aesthetics also has an eco logical link, with trees as symbols of nature and linking to changes in the relation ship between the human and natural worlds.

findings.consequent: City woods closed off for hunting/recreation
findings.quote: Power relationships have been reflected, for example, in rulers and the elite clos ing off city woods for their own (hunting and recreational) benefit (Fig. 1.2).

findings.consequent: Important 'place enhancers'
findings.quote: In this process, trees are often important ‘place enhancers’, as in the case of this Italian city square

findings.antecedent: Social interactions, experiences, and memories within a place
findings.consequent: Stronger connections with places, sense of place
findings.quote: connections with places are often strongest and most compelling when rooted in social interactions within a place, with the sense of a place deriving from people, experiences and memories created in the place (Ardoin 2005).

findings.antecedent: City forests (presence of trees, closed/open, light/dark, contrast to hurried life, place to disconnect/contemplate)
findings.consequent: Defined as place for people/animals/plants, contrast to civilised/cultivated, preferred with limited facilities/people
findings.quote: Interviewees saw the forest as a contrast to hurried life, as a place to ‘disconnect’ and to contemplate. For some, the forest acted as contrast to the civilised and culti vated. Most people preferred a limited amount of facilities as well as other people in the forest (Oustrup 2007).

findings.consequent: Feeling caught up/carried along, filled/inspired, personal growth, self-reflection
findings.quote: A spiritual experience is an intuitive and emotional kind of experience in which a person feels caught up and carried along – or alternatively filled and inspired – by a feeling, an idea, an image or a creative impulse. This can be through religious rituals and disciplines, but also through contact with forests or other parts of the natural environment.

findings.consequent: Symbolic reflection of unconscious, undefinable, essence of life/existence
findings.quote: The forest has been an important archetype, for example, symbolically reflect ing the basic structure of the unconscious, the undefinable, and the essence of life and existence (Schroeder 1992; Koch 1997).

findings.consequent: Feelings of fear, exclusion
findings.quote: Jones and Cloke (2002) mention that ‘places of trees’ can be places of fear as well as of exclusion.

findings.consequent: Preferred for hunting, refuge
findings.quote: The prospect-refuge theory proposed by Appleton (1996) suggests that our ances tors preferred the half-open landscape of the savannah where they could hunt for prey. The forest edge was also important, however, as it provided the necessary refuge.

findings.antecedent: Criminal behavior of other humans, secluded nature of forest, remoteness
findings.consequent: Forest fears
findings.quote: Many forest fears are not caused by the forest itself, but rather by criminal behav iour of other human beings who use the forest, its secluded nature, and relative remoteness as a cover.

findings.consequent: Feelings of unsafety
findings.quote: Half of the respondents answered that they felt unsafe or not really safe in the most densely vegetated part of the forest (Nibbering and Van Geel 1993).

findings.consequent: Increased excitement, courage, self-confidence
findings.quote: certain feelings of fear can be ‘turned around’ to add to the excitement of the city forest experience (Van den Berg and Ter Heijne 2004). Visitors can be surprised by the unknown and find new courage and self-confidence.

findings.consequent: Important role in building city states/nation states (source of timber/fuelwood)
findings.quote: City forests in played a particularly important role in the building of first city states and later nation states, as they pro vided a nearby source of timber and fuelwood.

findings.consequent: Increased municipal forest ownership
findings.quote: As forest ownership offers arguably the best means of controlling what happens with the forest, this increased interference also gave rise to more municipal forest ownership.

findings.consequent: Symbolic value in democratisation/revolutions
findings.quote: Trees sometimes had important symbolic value in democratisation processes and revolutions, as in the case of the Lombardy poplar (Populus nigra L.), which became a much-revered symbol of the French Revolution.

findings.consequent: Increased property values, important factor for buying a house
findings.quote: Nearby green space can have a significant effect on property values. People consider having green space nearby as an important argument for buying a house...

findings.consequent: Perceived as safe/familiar 'places' and unpredictable/exciting/unknown 'spaces'
findings.quote: city forests are both safe, familiar ‘places’ and unpre dictable, exciting and sometimes challenging and unknown ‘spaces’.

findings.consequent: Constitute a bounded other world (childhood dens, woodland garden), associated with spirituality/transcendence
findings.quote: For people, woodlands may constitute a bounded other world, the world of child hood dens, a woodland garden (Jorgensen and Anthopoulou 2007). They may be associated with spirituality and transcendence (see Chap. 2 ‘The Spiritual Forest’).

findings.consequent: Used for walking, cycling, jogging, sports; provide nature experience, 'getting away'
findings.quote: Most city forests are primarily used for walking, cycling, jogging, and other sports activities. Experiencing nature and just ‘getting away’ also score high when people are asked for their motivations to visit (city) forests.

findings.consequent: Feelings of happy, relaxed, close to nature
findings.quote: Visitors of the woodlands of the town of Redditch, United Kingdom most frequently expressed the emotions of feeling happy, relaxed, and close to nature (Coles and Bussey 2000).

findings.antecedent: Cities offering 'escape opportunities' and places for adventures
findings.consequent: Important for teenagers (and others)
findings.quote: Accounts such as those of the Scottish teenagers (Thompson et al. 2006) show, however, that it is important for cities to offer ‘escape opportunities’ and to provide places that allow for adventures.

findings.consequent: Source of inspiration for artists/writers
findings.quote: Artists and writers were among the first to stress the importance of forests and nature in general as source of inspiration.

findings.consequent: Bridges rift between different views of nature/forests
findings.quote: In this context, the role of the artist is that of a mediator and enabler. In fact, this has always been an important role of the artist, who had to ‘bridge’ the rift between different views of nature and forests.

findings.consequent: High variety of plant and animal species (biodiversity hotspots)
findings.quote: Various studies have confirmed that urban areas often harbour a perhaps surpris ingly high variety of species of plants and animals (e.g. Cornelis and Hermy 2004; Gustavsson et al. 2005; Alvey 2006; Lorusso et al. 2007; Nielsen et al. 2014).

findings.consequent: Widely varying cognitive, ethical, and aesthetic valuation perspectives of nature
findings.quote: The cognitive, ethical and aesthetic ‘valuation perspectives’ of nature held by different groups and individuals vary widely in modern Western society, where there no longer are certain fixed, leading principles.

findings.consequent: Particular need for 'wild adventure space'
findings.quote: young people seem to have a particular need for ‘wild adventure space’.

findings.antecedent: Sedentary lifestyles, psychological stress (urban living/work), climate change, air pollution, environmental hazards
findings.consequent: Poor health
findings.quote: Contributing factors to poor health include increasingly sedentary lifestyles, growing levels of psychological stress associated with urban living and contempo rary work practices, climate change, and exposure to air pollution and other environ mental hazards (Nilsson et al. 2007b; Van den Bosch 2017; Van den Bosch and Ode Sang 2017).

findings.antecedent: Natural outdoor areas (forests, parks, gardens, trees)
findings.consequent: Enhanced public health and well-being
findings.quote: Natural outdoor areas and natural elements such as forests, parks, gardens, and trees are known to provide opportunities for interactions that enhance public health and well-being (Stigsdotter and Grahn 2002; Nilsson et al. 2007b; Van den Bosch 2017; Van den Bosch and Ode Sang 2017).

findings.consequent: Changes in immune markers, reduced stress hormones, lowered blood glucose levels (for diabetics)
findings.quote: Studies have measured changes in immune markers and stress hormones in people who regularly walked in specific forests. In addition, people with diabetes but not taking insulin found substantial benefits by lowering blood glucose levels (e.g. Park et al. 2010; Tyrväinen et al. 2014).

findings.consequent: Reduced stress, anger, frustration, aggression; enhanced social safety; reduced aggressive behavior/criminal activity
findings.quote: Evidence suggests that exposure to natural envi ronments may reduce feelings of anger, frustration, and aggression. In turn, this may enhance feelings of social safety, and even reduce actual rates of aggressive behaviour and criminal activity (Groenewegen et al. 2006).

findings.consequent: Decreased depression, benefited mental health
findings.quote: Seventy-one percent of the respon dents reported a decrease in levels of depression after a walk in the park... Ninety-four percent of the respondents said that green activities had benefited their mental health, lifting depression.

findings.antecedent: Windows looking on forest scenery (for office workers)
findings.consequent: Lower levels of stress, higher job satisfaction
findings.quote: A study in South Korea indicated that office workers with windows looking on forest scenery have lower levels of stress and higher job satisfaction (Shin 2007).

findings.consequent: Educational roles ('Forests of Learning')
findings.quote: Over time, city forests have had various educational roles, and thus these forests can be considered as Forests of Learning.

findings.antecedent: Young children walking through forest with saws/tools
findings.consequent: Strong negative reaction from adults (parental concerns, liability rules)
findings.quote: participants from several other European countries reacted strongly when they saw young children walking through the forest with saws and other tools in their hands. This would never be possible at home, people said, because of parental concerns and the many rules and regulations concerning liabil ity.

findings.consequent: Adventurous 'wildscapes', places to hang out/escape from adults, exposure to nature (for children/youth)
findings.quote: Urban woodlands in many forms and shapes have provided children and youth with adventurous ‘wildscapes’, places to hang out and escape from adult eyes, as well as important exposure to nature.

findings.antecedent: Many indoor options (computers, IT), structured time, parental disinterest in nature
findings.consequent: Children spending less time in nature
findings.quote: Louv argues, we can see a worrying trend in many societies of children spending less time in nature, for example because there are many other options to spend one’s free time (and these are often indoors, such as using computers and other IT), children’s time has become more structured along organised school and other activities, and because parents are less interested in nature themselves.

findings.antecedent: Forest features (changing, unexplored action possibilities, ditches, loose branches, wildlife, water, variation, gradation)
findings.consequent: Children attracted to features, continually new affordances
findings.quote: Lerstrup concluded that that children are attracted to fea tures with changing and not yet fully explored action possibilities. She highlights, for example, ditches as offering especially rich affordances, but also items such as loose branches, wildlife, and water.

findings.antecedent: Children involved in forest management activities (creating own places in woodland)
findings.consequent: Developed creativity, understanding of forest, improved relations with each other
findings.quote: The researchers who studied the process noted that children developed their creativ ity, understanding of the forest, as well as relations with each other (Gunnarsson and Palenius 2004).

findings.consequent: Essential elements of healthy communities for children, integral part of urban planning (integrated at multiple scales)
findings.quote: trees and natural areas are essential ele ments of healthy communities for children. As a result, these green spaces need to become an integral part of urban planning, being integrated at multiple scales, from landscaping around homes, schools, and childcare centers, to linked systems of urban trails, greenways, parks, and wildscapes for children’s creative and adventur ous play.

findings.consequent: Important in 'place making'/'place keeping', providing local identity, meeting place, link between people/environment
findings.quote: Trees and forests have been important in ‘place making’ (and place keeping) by local communities, pro viding local identity, a meeting place and a link between people and their local environment.

findings.consequent: Landscape of importance for local and national identity
findings.quote: The wooded landscape of Vrelo Bosne, the source of the Bosne river near Sarajevo, is a landscape of importance for local and national identity

findings.antecedent: Access to city forests and green spaces
findings.consequent: Strengthened use of city forests, enhanced social interaction, better social cohesion, joint place-making, shaped community identity
findings.quote: Successful, joint place-making requires, first of all, that people have access to city forests and other green spaces... This strengthens the use of city forests by all parts of urban society, thereby enhancing opportunities for social interaction, better social cohesion, and ultimately, joint place-making and the shaping of community identity.

findings.consequent: Form a wide range of landscapes
findings.quote: The very definition of urban forest embraces diversity, recognising that trees can help form a wide range of landscapes, for example based on their density and prevalence.

findings.antecedent: Introduced species, socio-economic factors, land use/cover heterogeneity, environmental factor diversity (soil/climate)
findings.consequent: High species richness for urban flora
findings.quote: High species richness for urban flora has typically been explained by a combination of four factors: (i) the high incidence of intro duced species, (ii) socio-economic factors, (iii) land use and land cover heterogene ity, and (iv) diversity of environmental factors like soil and climate diversity (Alvey 2006).

findings.antecedent: Lack of information about forests, fear of nature (based on home country knowledge), feeling unwelcome
findings.consequent: Newcomers/cultural groups not visiting urban woodlands
findings.quote: Newcomers or people from specific cultural groups may simply lack information about the forests and the possibilities offered, or they may fear nature based on what they know about forests, wildlife etc. from their home countries... They can feel unwelcome to visit local urban woodland or other nature areas.

findings.consequent: Optimized multiple ecosystem services, ensured urban forest stability (but not guaranteed improved ecosystem function)
findings.quote: Although high species diversity can optimize multiple ecosystem services and ensure urban forest stability in the face of disturbance, words of caution are needed. Urban foresters cannot only manage for diversity, as increasing tree species diver sity by itself does not guarantee improved ecosystem function.

findings.antecedent: Large interests in city forests (place making, societal demands)
findings.consequent: Common conflicts of interests
findings.quote: Given the large interests in city forests, for example because of their role in place making, and the many societal demands, it is obvious that conflicts of interests are common.

findings.antecedent: Conflict management (using positive dimensions, reducing negative impacts)
findings.consequent: Situation improvement
findings.quote: Conflict management is about making use of the positive dimensions of conflicts and reducing the negative impacts... Conflict management, they say, is aimed at situation improvement.

findings.antecedent: Appropriate conflict management strategy, people's commitment to forest
findings.consequent: Avoided escalation of conflict, withstood political pressures, raised resources for forest management
findings.quote: With an appropriate conflict management strategy, esca lation in the Forest of Conflict can be avoided. Moreover, people’s commitment to the forest can be used for the better. It can help withstand political pressures to convert city forests to other land use, for example, and raise resources to support forest management.

findings.antecedent: Green infrastructure (integrative planning of multifunctional green spaces)
findings.consequent: Urban renaissance, green space regeneration, met environmental/social/economic needs of community
findings.quote: It can be defined as creating net works of multifunctional green spaces that are carefully planned to meet the envi ronmental, social and economic needs of a community.

findings.consequent: Important roles in place making, providing identities to communities/cities/countries
findings.quote: Trees, city forests and other green spaces play important roles in place making by individuals as well as groups... City forests have helped provide identities to communities, cities and sometimes even countries.

findings.consequent: Supplement/contrast to 'artificial' nature representations in cities
findings.quote: City forests, old and new, offer a much-needed supplement and perhaps even contrast to the more ‘artificial’ representations of nature that tend to dominate our cities and towns.

findings.consequent: Forestry increasingly dominated, becoming 'urban' (responding to urban perceptions/needs)
findings.quote: forestry at large is increasingly dominated by urban societies and their values, norms and demands... all forestry is becoming urban in the sense that it must respond to urban perceptions and needs.

limitations: Geographical bias towards Northern and Northwestern Europe, though mitigated in the second edition (p. 8, 23).
Lack of scientific evidence on the precise mechanisms of nature-health linkages (p. 141).
Green space is often perceived as a luxury rather than a necessity, especially in urban areas with fierce competition for land (p. 141).
Parental concerns and liability rules limit children's engagement in 'wild' play in forests (p. 156).
Wild adventure space is poorly understood and associated with safety concerns among adults (p. 160).
Decreasing outdoor time for children due to lack of national policies for 'outdoor' days in schools (p. 165).
Unequal access to public green space in many cities for certain segments of the population (p. 176).
Species diversity alone does not guarantee improved ecosystem function in urban forests (p. 192).
Lack of knowledge about the impact of increasing human diversity on urban forest use and planning (p. 193).
Financial struggles in metropolitan cores, leading to dereliction of buildings and infrastructure (p. 220).
Risk of distorted nature views from 'de-contextualised, idealised' nature representations in theme parks (p. 224).
Decline in visits to forest and nature by young people and ethnic minorities (p. 229).
minimum_safe_summary: This book, 'The Forest and the City,' by Cecil C. Konijnendijk, is a narrative review and conceptual framework that explores the cultural and social dimensions of urban forests. It argues that city forests are complex cultural landscapes, serving as both familiar 'places' and adventurous 'spaces,' deeply intertwined with human identity, spirituality, and well-being. Key findings highlight that urban forests have historically provided essential resources, served as sites of power and prestige, offered recreational escapes, inspired art, and contributed to physical and mental health. They are crucial for children's development and community building, but their use is influenced by diverse cultural views and often hampered by fears and conflicts. The book emphasizes the need for socially-inclusive planning and management to leverage city forests for creating more sustainable and liveable urban environments. Limitations include a historical bias towards Northern European examples and a recognized lack of scientific evidence on the precise mechanisms of nature-health linkages.
